title: Love and argument
hookLine: Jews hold many views on Israel's politics; some love it, some criticize it, some do both

lines: A COUSIN, AN UNCLE, A GRANDMOTHER.
cards: A Shabbat dinner table. The candles are lit, the bread is blessed, and somewhere around the soup someone mentions Israel's government. One cousin is furious at it.
An uncle defends it, louder. A grandmother says she loves the country and is worried sick about it. Somebody's new partner, at the table for the first time, wonders whether to say anything at all.
Nobody leaves. The arguing goes on through the chicken. Dessert still comes.

teach.b: Ask Jews about Israel's politics and you will hear many views. Some love the country and defend its choices. Some love it and criticize it hard.

teach.h: THESE AND THESE ARE WORDS OF GOD.
teach.b: Some do several of these at once. Arguing hard is not new in this tradition. The Talmud is built out of disagreements, with the losing side's view kept on the page.

The house of Hillel and the house of Shammai, two schools of rabbis, argued for years. The Talmud says a heavenly voice finally declared that both were the words of the living God, but the law would follow Hillel.
Why Hillel? Because, the Talmud says, they were kind and humble, and they taught Shammai's view too, even putting it before their own.
The Mishnah draws a line through all arguing: an argument for the sake of heaven will last; one that isn't, won't. Its good example: Hillel and Shammai.
Its bad one: Korah and his followers, who argued with Moses to grab power.

teach.h: LOVE AND REBUKE IN ONE VERSE.
teach.b: And the Torah puts love and honest challenge in a single verse. It begins, "Thou shalt not hate thy brother in thy heart," and in the same breath tells you to speak up when your neighbor does wrong.

Read that way, criticism and love are not opposites, and keeping quiet can be a way of giving up on someone. The question is the Mishnah's: is this for the sake of heaven, to understand, or just to win?
This lesson won't tell you what to think about Israel. It describes a very old way of arguing: loudly, honestly, at the same table, staying for dessert.

how: Jews study Talmud in pairs, called chavruta, arguing over the text together, and the Mishnah's ideal of an argument 'for the sake of heaven' is often cited for disagreements in the community.

games.q: two schools of rabbis have argued for years. a heavenly voice says both are the words of the living God, but the law will follow one of them. why that one?
o: they were kind and humble, and taught the other side's view first.
games.why: the Talmud says the law follows the house of Hillel because they were kind and humble, and taught Shammai's words, even before their own.

practice: Bring to mind one person who sees something important very differently from you, in politics, faith or family, and picture them across a table.
Let them speak first, and try to say their view back in a way they'd call fair, the way the house of Hillel taught the other side's words. You don't have to agree; just listen until you understand.

wordCard.voice: Hillel, whose school argued for years with Shammai's, and whose kindness and humility won the law's final word.

orig.note: Hebrew: for the sake of heaven, the Mishnah's test for a good argument.

carryVoice: Your line: love and argue. Both views stay on the page, and everyone stays at the table. Until tomorrow.
